summary: We chose this specific NASA challenge because it touches upon one of the most critical questions of modern space exploration: How can we test our robots, scientific instruments, spacesuits, and the durability of our materials for Mars, before launching them millions of kilometers away? Initially, the challenge seemed particularly exciting and, at first glance, relatively simple, as we were not scientists but mathematicians, programmers, electrical engineers, and physicists. We believed it would be enough to locate a few deserts or icy landscapes that visually "resemble" the Red Planet. However, as soon as we delved into the actual data from NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA), we realized that the endeavor was extremely demanding and multidimensional. No spot on Earth is identical to Mars; Mars is a world of extreme cold, huge thermal fluctuations, minimal atmospheric pressure, high radiation, and distinct geochemistry. This exact complexity motivated us even more, transforming our initial curiosity into a rigorous, methodical scientific research.
details: From the very first moment of designing our proposal, we set a fundamental rule: space science and planetary exploration should not be the privilege of a closed group of experts, but a common property, understandable and accessible to everyone. For this reason, our work is not only addressed to the scientific evaluation committee, but mainly to the broad, non-specialized public — to school students, university students, citizens of all ages, as well as to people with disabilities (PwD), such as people with visual or hearing impairments. We wanted to create a comprehensive experience that translates complex astrophysical, geological, and climatological data into tangible, experiential knowledge, so that everyone can understand how we prepare on Earth for humanity's next steps on Mars.
